timeText:
How many of you have been in the middle of a fight and thought, I wish I could just show you the whole conversation. Not my screenshot. The whole thing.
I thought about that a lot. So I built it.

A friend came to me after a fight with someone she cared about. She was certain she was right. She had the screenshots. She had replayed it enough times that her version felt like fact.

I asked her to export the chat and drop it into something I had been quietly building.

Twenty minutes later she went quiet.

Not because she was wrong. Not because she was right either. Just because seeing the whole thing, every message, every gap, every time she reached out and every time she didn't, looked very different from inside the fight.

That's ThreadLens. You upload a WhatsApp, Telegram, or iMessage export. Nothing leaves your browser. No account needed. You see who messages first, who waits longer, who says sorry more, who escalates. Patterns across the whole thread, not just the part you're angry about right now.

There's an optional AI if you want to ask it something in your own words. It only sees what you ask about.

It's free. I just think we'd argue less if we looked at the record before we looked for someone to blame.

timeText:
HackerRank literally open-sourced their ATS!!!!

I replied to a rejection email once.

Not a polished follow-up. Not a "thank you for your time" message.

A frustrated, borderline unhinged email to HackerRank asking them straight up.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐠𝐮𝐲𝐬 𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐨𝐫?
Good Ranks. Contest Ratings. Deployed Projects. Good CGPA. Experience.
𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐦𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠? 𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐦𝐞??

I did not expect a reply. I expected to be ignored.

Instead, Harishankaran Karunanidhi, Co-founder & CTO of HackerRank, replied personally.

And what he said changed how I think about hiring forever.

𝑯𝒆 𝒅𝒊𝒅 𝒏𝒐𝒕 𝒆𝒙𝒑𝒍𝒂𝒊𝒏 𝒎𝒚 𝒓𝒆𝒋𝒆𝒄𝒕𝒊𝒐𝒏.
𝑯𝒆 𝒂𝒔𝒌𝒆𝒅 𝒎𝒆 𝒕𝒐 𝒓𝒖𝒏 𝒎𝒚 𝒓𝒆𝒔𝒖𝒎𝒆 𝒂𝒈𝒂𝒊𝒏𝒔𝒕 𝒕𝒉𝒆𝒊𝒓 𝑨𝑻𝑺.

Their entire hiring agent is open sourced on GitHub.

Not a black box. Not some vague rubric nobody sees. An actual AI agent you can run your resume through yourself and see exactly how it scores you.

𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐡𝐢𝐭 𝐦𝐞 𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐝:

Gone are the days when a decent CGPA, a todo app on GitHub, and a LeetCode streak got you through the door.

Companies are running AI agents on your resume now. Those agents are not impressed by checkboxes. They are looking for depth, for signal, for proof that you can actually build and think.

𝑩𝒂𝒔𝒊𝒄 𝑫𝑺𝑨. 𝑩𝒂𝒔𝒊𝒄 𝒑𝒓𝒐𝒋𝒆𝒄𝒕𝒔. 𝑩𝒂𝒔𝒊𝒄 𝒑𝒓𝒐𝒇𝒊𝒍𝒆.
𝒀𝒆𝒉 𝒔𝒃 𝒑𝒆𝒉𝒍𝒆 𝒔𝒆 𝒉𝒊 𝒌𝒂𝒇𝒊 𝒏𝒂𝒉𝒊𝒏 𝒕𝒉𝒂. 𝑨𝒃 𝒕𝒐 𝒃𝒊𝒍𝒌𝒖𝒍 𝒏𝒂𝒉𝒊𝒏 𝒉𝒂𝒊.

The bar has moved. And most people are still preparing for the old bar.

Link to the open source hiring agent is in the comments. Run your resume through it. See what an AI actually thinks of you before a recruiter does.

It is uncomfortable. Do it anyway.

Ciao 🫡

timeText:
Quant Research / Quant Trading / Applied Science / ML Quant interviews are an enigma. You read the green book. You grind fifty challenging probability problems. You memorize the birthday problem, the gambler's ruin, Monty Hall. And then you sit down at a Jane Street or HRT or Citadel and they hit you with a trading game, expected value games etc. you've never seen before and none of your memorized answers help.

The problem isn't a lack of puzzles. It's that puzzles can come from any angle. The attack vectors are so varied that even after months of prep, you can stare at a problem and have no idea which path to take. Should you condition on the first step? Set up a recurrence? Look for a martingale? Draw a geometric region? The answer is always "obvious" in hindsight but finding it under pressure in real time is a completely different skill. That's the gap I tried to close.

I wrote a long form blog post w/ Claude Opus that doesn't just teach puzzles, it teaches you how to recognize which technique a problem is asking for before you've solved it. 13 techniques. 30+ worked problems. A recognition flowchart at the end for pattern matching new problems on sight.

This weekend, sit down with a notebook, a pen and your phone on silent. Pick a puzzle, not necessarily in the order I've presented them and try to solve it before reading the solution. I've chosen the puzzles I think are famous enough and instructive enough to make the initial list but I've certainly missed most of them doing the rounds. If there's a puzzle you think belongs here, drop it in the comments. I'll keep updating this as a living compendium.

I reduced the token usage of Claude Code and Cursor by ~60% with a small command line tool


Although we don't cap the token usage in our company, it's always good to keep an eye on how much we actually spend on tokens. Since we are heavily using AI in Development, reducing the tokens and therefor the amount we pay while still getting the same results is a no-brainer.

Reza, one of my employees, mentioned this tool "rtk" recently and I tried it out immediately.

How it works:
It's a small CLI that rewrites Bash commands (e.g. git status becomes rtk git status) before execution. This provides compact output to the agent without needing to call rtk explicitly.

It's open source. The link to the repo is in the first comment.

(I've only been testing it for a couple of days so far but 60% is impressive)

Reflecting on an incredible experience at the Graviton Crucible Challenge earlier this month! 🚀

Here’s a look back at the highlights:

Phase 1: The Runtime Challenge
It started at the IIT Delhi campus with a grueling individual challenge. No maps, no hints, just pure logic, C++, and system design. Qualifying for the "Inner Circle" (the top 100) was just the beginning.

Phase 2: The Crucible (The Main Arena)
The offline event was where things truly leveled up. I’m thrilled to share that I managed to secure 1st Place in two of the major challenges:

🏆 BrainBlitz (The Kahoot Quiz): Out of 100+ participants, I finished Rank 1. This was a rapid-fire test of Math, Probability, Statistics, C++, and Finance. It was all about having the right intuition under immense time pressure.

📈 Live Trading Round: My teammate, Tushar Kumar Sinha, and I (Team Positron) had a wild ride. We were sitting at 5th place after the second round, but we stayed calm, adjusted our strategy based on the news cycles, and managed to climb to Rank 1 by the third round, holding that top spot until the very end!

The Learning Curve

Beyond the competition, the masterclasses were a massive highlight. Learning directly from Graviton Quant Researchers about strategies like order book imbalance, mean reversion strategies, momentum signals, etc and then applying those concepts in the Algorithmic Trading challenge was an eye-opener. It wasn’t just about coding; it was about building a framework that could survive the noise of a live market.

Final Thoughts

The day ended with some great informal chats with the Graviton team. Hearing their "unfiltered" insights into the world of quant was invaluable. It’s rare to find an event that balances high-level competition with such genuine mentorship.

A huge thank you to Diksha Singh, Ashish Banga, and Tanya Makhija for organizing such a seamless and high-octane event. And of course, a shoutout to Graviton Research Capital LLP for opening the doors to the Crucible!

Grateful for the wins, but even more for the perspective.

The book explores a range of topics across five parts, from intuitive quant like behavioral finance, to applied models such as portfolio optimization, and deeper ideas in mathematical and stochastic finance. 

Along the way, we’ve tried to go beyond standard explanations, revisiting these ideas through careful study, clearer intuition, and in some cases small twists or extensions to the usual implementations.

Our aim is simple: make niche quant concepts more accessible and spark curiosity for the field.

Usually it takes 70-80 ounces of silver to buy 1 ounce of gold

This relationship is known as the gold-silver ratio
And throughout history the ratio has averaged roughly 73
But markets rarely stay near equilibrium.

As part of an ongoing series of small quantitative studies on commodity markets, I examined how the ratio behaves after statistically significant deviations from its long-run mean.

Using daily futures data, the analysis focused on:
• the historical distribution of the gold–silver ratio
• deviation thresholds defined by standard deviation bands
• the persistence of extreme dislocations
• forward silver returns following these events

Some observations from the study:
• The long-run mean sits near 73 with a standard deviation around 14.
• The current ratio lies close to the 20th percentile of historical observations.
• Extreme deviations tend to persist longer than simple mean-reversion assumptions suggest.
• When the ratio exceeds +1σ, silver has historically produced stronger returns over the following 30–90 trading day horizons.

The results suggest that while the ratio does revert over time, the adjustment process is slow and highly unpredictable. 

Equilibrium in markets is real
But patience is the price of convergence.
